title: El Salvador TPS Holds Past Its Deadline as Employers Await DHS Guidance
excerpt: The designation's September 9 expiry passed with no Federal Register notice from DHS, leaving beneficiaries protected but employers without updated I-9 instructions.
body:
• El Salvador's TPS designation was scheduled to end on September 9, 2026, but DHS has not published a termination or extension notice in the Federal Register.
  • USCIS and E-Verify have posted guidance saying a further announcement will be issued and that Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries continue to retain TPS protections, including employment authorization, in the meantime.
  • Employers face a documentation gap: no updated expiration dates or Form I-9 instructions have been issued for the interim period.
  • Immigration counsel advise against automatically extending I-9 expiration dates by six months without government guidance, and recommend documenting interim compliance decisions.

A Deadline Arrives Without a Decision

Employers with Salvadoran workers on Temporary Protected Status are navigating an unusual compliance situation. El Salvador's current TPS period was scheduled to end on September 9, 2026, but as of that date, the Department of Homeland Security had not published a termination or extension notice in the Federal Register, according to immigration law firm WR Immigration.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=SJfB9gdyY50

Instead, USCIS and E-Verify have posted guidance indicating that a further announcement regarding El Salvador TPS will be issued and that, in the meantime, Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries continue to retain TPS protections, including employment authorization. That provides important reassurance on the substance — workers remain protected and authorized — while leaving open the practical question of how that authorization should be documented on Form I-9.

Why the Timing Matters

The TPS statute requires DHS to periodically review whether the conditions supporting a country's designation continue to exist. If DHS decides to end a designation, termination generally cannot take effect earlier than 60 days after the termination notice is published in the Federal Register, under INA §244(b)(3)(B). If DHS does not determine that a country no longer meets the requirements, the designation continues for at least another six months, with DHS holding discretion to extend for 12 or 18 months instead, under INA §244(b)(3)(C).

Recent DHS practice shows a delayed announcement does not always lead to the same result. When Honduras TPS was scheduled to expire in July 2025, DHS announced the termination after the stated expiration date and set a later effective termination date consistent with the statutory transition period. By contrast, when DHS could not make the required determination for South Sudan by the statutory deadline in 2025, it expressly announced an automatic six-month extension and issued a Federal Register notice addressing the continued validity of TPS-related employment authorization documentation. For El Salvador, no comparable formal guidance has yet appeared, and that absence is what is creating uncertainty for employers.

"Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries currently remain protected and employment authorized, but employers are still waiting for the government to explain how that continuation should be documented for Form I-9 purposes."

— WR Immigration analysis

What Employers Should Do Now

WR Immigration advises employers to separate two questions: whether the employee continues to have TPS and employment authorization, and what documentation permits the employer to reflect that authorization on Form I-9. The first is answered by current government messaging; the second remains unclear without updated I-9 instructions, EAD validity dates, or a Federal Register notice.

Its recommended steps include identifying affected employees now, not assuming the prior expiration date requires termination of employment, avoiding automatic six-month I-9 extensions without supporting guidance, documenting the decision-making process with copies of the relevant USCIS and E-Verify guidance, monitoring the Federal Register, USCIS, E-Verify and SAVE closely, and applying any review consistently — driven by documented expiration dates and government guidance rather than nationality or assumptions about status.

The "Automatic Extension" Caution

Although INA §244(b)(3)(C) provides a statutory mechanism for continuing a designation when DHS makes no determination, employers should be careful about translating that provision directly into an I-9 expiration date. Historically, when DHS has relied on an automatic extension, it has issued formal guidance addressing the designation and the associated employment authorization documentation — South Sudan being the recent example. Here, DHS has not yet done so. Until it does, employers should avoid assumptions about new expiration dates, preserve documentation supporting interim compliance decisions, and work with immigration counsel on whether and how to continue employment for affected workers.
